Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette: James Sullivan, a 46-year-old graphic designer with a calm, methodical habit, had never imagined his life would be punctuated by the flashing blue of a police cruiser. On a rainy Thursday evening in late October, while he was walking home from a late client deadline, a police officer stopped him at a crosswalk that had, according to James's memory, been empty for months. The officer demanded that James pull over, but James, certain that he had been following the streetlights, stepped off the curb and began to walk, his hand instinctively reaching for the envelope of a design file tucked into his jacket. The officer's knuckles pressed on the car door, his face turned from confusion to anger, and before James could even ask why he was being stopped, a hand shoved his shoulder, a sharp hiss of rubber, and a sudden, painful sting as a hand struck his face. The officer's boots, with their dark, scuffed soles, seemed to echo the harshness of the moment. He felt a rush of fear, the kind that makes the heart pound and the vision blur, and when the siren's wail faded into a distant drone, he was left alone on the pavement, clutching a broken smartphone screen, bruised in places he could not immediately name. From that night forward, James's world narrowed to the images and sounds that had defined his trauma. The intrusive thought of a police officer's glare came unbidden when he passed a courthouse, the sight of a child with a torn sleeve on a school bus triggered an immediate recollection of a hand slamming against his own arm, and the very presence of an authority figure-any uniformed person-caused his chest to tighten. These triggers did not simply remind him of the event; they lit a fire in his mind, generating a state of threat. He could not relax, no matter how far from the scene he was, and he constantly mapped escape routes in his mind before he could feel safe, even at his office. In the dim glow of his studio, with a whiteboard full of color swatches and a monitor displaying client logos, his body stayed taut, fingers on the mouse hovering, the muscles of his neck and shoulders ready to respond to a danger that never truly left. The memory of the assault seeped into his life in waves that overwhelmed him. When the memory returned, James felt so much emotion-anger, fear, humiliation-that he would freeze mid-sentence, unable to finish explaining what had happened to anyone. He could not clearly describe the officer's face or the exact force of the shove; the narrative tangled like a knot in his mind, leaving him feeling helpless. The mere thought that someone might not believe his version of events, that the system had failed him, seemed to make the memory even more vivid. James had begun to think that the injustice of the incident was a wound that would never heal; the idea that his life had been destroyed by a single act of violence left him feeling as if every color he ever chose was meaningless. Because of these intrusive triggers and the sense of threat that followed, James turned to maladaptive strategies that he had learned from other stressful moments. He began to spend long hours on his phone, scrolling through memes or playing endless rounds of a puzzle game, to keep his mind occupied and to avoid thinking about the officer's hand. Whenever he felt a flash of a face or heard a siren, he would immediately pull the device out and dive into a stream of social media content, forcing the brain to stay in the present of the screen rather than the present of the past. He also started to avoid other people, refusing to join colleagues for lunch or to attend team meetings, believing that any group setting might bring up authority figures or strangers who could provoke his memories. These avoidance tactics, while offering temporary relief, only deepened the cycle. The longer he stayed in the safety of his screen, the more the memories resurfaced with intensity, and the more he felt threatened by the world outside his studio. James's negative appraisals compounded this loop. He came to believe that his life had been irreparably damaged; that the world was a hostile place where people could strike without consequence. These beliefs did not just accompany the threat-they amplified it. When a sudden siren drifted through the office hallway, the sense of impending danger rose, and he felt the same tightness in his shoulders he had felt on that rainy night. The memory of the officer's hand became a constant reminder that the world was unforgiving, and his attempt to escape through screen time only reinforced the perception that reality was dangerous and that he was powerless to change it. In the months that followed, the maladaptive strategies became habits. When James returned to his work, he found himself scrolling through a game for hours, his laptop screen becoming a refuge. He avoided coworkers, which strained his marriage; his wife, Maria, began to feel neglected and frustrated by his isolation. The constant tension made him anxious, and he began to dread even the sight of a police badge, fearing that a simple stop could trigger a flood of memories. By the time he reached out for help, he was exhausted, his sense of meaning extinguished, and his life seemed to have little hope of recovery. The last spark that brought him to therapy was the realization that he could no longer live on autopilot; each day he woke, he was terrified that a passing siren would snap him back into that dark, violent memory. He was most afraid that the cycle would never break, but he also clung to a fragile hope that a professional might help him untangle the tangled web of his mind and restore even a sliver of peace.
